name: Army Brown
lede: Army Brown is a medium, warm brown, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary as first used in 1912, and among the most common colors in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: A name in the library
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates this brown to 1912, plate 6, swatch A 10, and separately catalogues a close match as "Rosario" in 1927 [1]. Despite the name, nothing in the sources here ties the color to any military use; the word may simply describe a drab, practical brown [1]. The nearest color-graph neighbor is [[cocoa]], 3.0 units away, with [[dusty-sienna]] close behind at 3.5, and [[rood-s-brown]] and [[yellowish-brown]] almost as close [2].

Munsell notation gives 4.8YR 4.5/5.1, a mid-lightness, moderately saturated yellow-brown [1]. The hex #926142 is a screen approximation; no dye or pigment sample survives in the record [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is an unusually common color in our archive: 2,067 of 23,781 paintings, about 8.7 percent, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the medieval and early Renaissance centuries, with the 1200s and 1300s both showing roughly two and a half times the archive's average rate [3]. The single sharpest concentration is the 1270s, nearly four and a half times average [3]. Pontormo, Otto van Veen, Christen Dalsgaard, Rosa Bonheur and Filippo Lippi all use it well above their peers' rates [3]. The strongest individual matches include Japanese ink paintings: Konoe Nobutada's *Tenjin Traveling to China* (1610) and two works by Shokadō Shōjō from 1600 [3]. All counts are computed matches on photographed, varnished canvases [3].
